cues: "Brace appropriately for each position" · "ribs down overhead, level on the suitcase" · "smooth transitions, stay tall"
mistakes: Arching the back on the overhead portion; tipping during the suitcase; losing posture in transitions; rushing
progression: Progress: heavier loads or longer segments | Regress: lighter loads, fewer positions, or shorter distances
muscles: Grip/forearms, traps, deltoids, obliques, quadratus lumborum, core, glutes

name: Rotational Med Ball Toss
execution: Stand side-on to a wall in an athletic stance, holding a med ball at the trunk. Wind up by rotating back into the trail hip, then explosively rotate the hips and trunk to whip the ball forward into the wall, finishing with the hips turned through. Catch or retrieve and reset. Drive the rotation from the ground up — hips, then trunk, then arms. Reps each side.
why: Trains explosive rotational power through the proper kinetic sequence — force initiates at the ground, transfers through the rotating hips and trunk, and finishes through the arms; the ballistic throw develops rate of force development in the rotational chain.
transfer: Directly mirrors the rotational power sequence of the wrist and slap shot and hard passing — loading the hips and unwinding through the trunk; trains the hip-to-trunk power transfer that drives shot velocity and rotational force.
cues: "Load the back hip, then unwind" · "drive ground-hips-trunk-arms" · "whip the ball, finish through"
mistakes: Throwing with the arms only (no hip drive); not loading the back hip; rotating from the lumbar instead of the hips; a soft, non-ballistic throw
progression: Progress: heavier ball or more explosive/farther | Regress: lighter ball or slower technical reps

name: Rotational Med Ball Side Toss
execution: Stand side-on to a wall, athletic stance, holding the med ball low and to the trail side. Wind into the back hip, then explosively rotate and toss the ball sideways into the wall with a scooping/side motion, driving through the hips and trunk. Retrieve, reset, and repeat. Emphasize the hip-driven rotation and a powerful, ballistic release. Reps each side.
why: Trains rotational and lateral power through a side-tossing pattern, emphasizing the hip-and-trunk drive into a horizontal release; develops rate of force development in the rotational chain with a release angle that loads the obliques and hips ballistically.
transfer: Mirrors the rotational, hip-driven power of shooting and hard passing and the lateral trunk power used to transfer force across the body; trains the explosive unwinding that drives shot and pass velocity.
cues: "Load the hip, scoop and explode" · "hips lead, trunk follows" · "ballistic release, finish through"
mistakes: An arms-only toss; no hip load; lumbar rotation instead of hip-driven; a soft release
progression: Progress: heavier ball or more explosive | Regress: lighter ball or technical-speed reps

name: Med-Ball Chest Pass (Wall)
execution: Stand facing a wall in an athletic stance, holding a med ball at the chest. Explosively press/throw the ball into the wall as hard as possible (like a basketball chest pass), then catch the rebound and immediately reset or repeat. Brace the trunk and use the legs slightly. Throw with maximal intent each rep, catching softly to absorb.
why: A ballistic horizontal press training maximal concentric velocity and rate of force development in the chest, shoulders, and triceps; the throw lets the athlete express pressing power without deceleration at the end, building explosive upper-body push.
transfer: Mirrors the explosive two-arm push used to shove opponents off the puck and create space in battles; builds the fast horizontal force production of the pressing muscles used in contact along the boards.
cues: "Punch the ball into the wall" · "athletic base, brace" · "catch soft, throw again"
mistakes: Throwing slowly (no power); all arms, no brace; not catching/absorbing the rebound; standing tall (no athletic base)
progression: Progress: heavier ball or add a step/load | Regress: lighter ball or closer to the wall

name: Banded Rotational Press
execution: Anchor a band to the side at chest height. In an athletic stance side-on, hold the band at the chest and press it forward while rotating the trunk and hips away from the anchor, finishing with the arms extended and the body turned through. Control the return. Drive the rotation from the hips through the trunk into the press. Reps each side.
why: Combines a horizontal press with trunk rotation against band resistance, training the rotational push pattern with accommodating load; the band lets the athlete train the press-and-rotate action with more control and time-under-tension than a ballistic throw, building rotational pressing strength.
transfer: Trains the combined rotate-and-push action used to transfer force into a shot or hard pass and to push through an opponent while rotating; builds the rotational pressing strength behind shooting power and protecting the puck with a turn-and-push.
cues: "Rotate from the hips and press" · "drive through, finish extended" · "control the return"
mistakes: Pressing without rotating (or vice versa); rotating from the low back; using arms only; letting the band snap back
progression: Progress: heavier band or more explosive | Regress: lighter band or smaller range
muscles: Obliques, pectorals, anterior deltoids, hips, core

name: Banded Rotational Throw (Wall)
execution: Anchor a band to the side. Hold it at the trunk in an athletic side-on stance, wind into the back hip against the band, then explosively rotate and release toward the wall — or drive into a hard rotational follow-through — driving the hips and trunk. Reset and repeat. Emphasize a ballistic, hip-driven rotation. Reps each side.
why: Trains explosive rotational power with band resistance, developing rate of force development in the rotational kinetic chain; the band’s accommodating resistance challenges the hip-and-trunk drive ballistically, reinforcing the ground-up sequence of rotational force production.
transfer: Mirrors the explosive rotational sequence of the wrist and slap shot and hard passing — loading the back hip and unwinding powerfully; trains the hip-to-trunk power transfer that drives shot and pass velocity.
cues: "Load the back hip, explode through" · "ground-hips-trunk, ballistic" · "finish turned through"
mistakes: An arms-only effort; no hip load; lumbar-driven rotation; a non-ballistic, slow effort
progression: Progress: heavier band or more explosive | Regress: lighter band or technical-speed reps

name: Band Rotational Scoop Toss
execution: Anchor a band low to the side. In an athletic stance, hold it low and to the trail side, wind into the back hip, then explosively rotate and “scoop” the band up and across the body diagonally (low-to-high), driving from the hips and legs through the trunk. Control back to the start. Reps each side. Emphasize the diagonal, ground-up power.
why: Trains diagonal (low-to-high) rotational power through the kinetic chain against band resistance; the scooping path emphasizes the combined hip extension and rotation used to transfer force diagonally across the body, building rotational and diagonal power with accommodating load.
transfer: Mirrors the diagonal, hip-driven power used to lift and rip a shot or make a hard pass — the low-to-high transfer of force from the legs and hips through the rotating trunk; trains the diagonal power behind elevating and driving the puck.
cues: "Scoop from the hips, low to high" · "drive the legs and hips, rotate through" · "control it back down"
mistakes: Using arms only; no leg/hip drive; rotating from the low back; a slow, non-explosive scoop
progression: Progress: heavier band or more explosive | Regress: lighter band or smaller range

name: DB Thruster
execution: Hold DBs racked at the shoulders, feet shoulder-width. Squat to at least parallel, then drive explosively up through the legs and, as the hips and knees extend, press the DBs overhead in one fluid motion, finishing with arms locked out and ribs down. Lower the DBs to the shoulders as you descend into the next squat. Repeat continuously.
why: A full-body compound that chains a squat into an overhead press, using leg drive to power the press (triple extension into the lockout); trains total-body strength, power transfer from legs through trunk to arms, and — at higher reps — conditioning.
transfer: Builds the full-body, ground-up power transfer and triple extension that underpin a powerful stride push-off and generating force from the legs through a braced trunk; the leg-to-overhead drive mirrors the explosive force transfer used in contact and battles.
cues: "Drive through the legs into the press" · "ribs down, finish tall" · "smooth squat-to-press rhythm"
mistakes: Pressing before the legs drive (no power transfer); arching the low back at lockout; squatting shallow; losing the rhythm
progression: Progress: heavier DBs or for power (low reps, max intent) | Regress: lighter DBs or split into squat + press

name: DB Complex
execution: Perform a series of DB exercises back-to-back without setting the weights down — for example, RDL → row → hang clean → front squat → press — completing the prescribed reps of each before flowing to the next. Keep the DBs in hand throughout, maintaining form as fatigue builds, then rest. Choose a load you can sustain across the whole sequence.
why: Chaining multiple compound lifts without rest creates a high total workload and metabolic demand while maintaining grip and postural control under accumulating fatigue; builds full-body strength-endurance, work capacity, and the ability to keep producing force when tired.
transfer: Builds the full-body strength-endurance and grip stamina to keep battling, pushing, and producing force late in shifts and games; training quality movement under fatigue mirrors maintaining strong skating and battling when tired.
cues: "Don’t set the DBs down" · "hold form as fatigue builds" · "smooth transitions between moves"
mistakes: Form breaking down under fatigue; choosing too heavy a load to sustain; rushing transitions sloppily; setting the weights down mid-complex
progression: Progress: heavier DBs, more reps, or more exercises | Regress: lighter DBs, fewer reps, or shorter complex
muscles: Full body (posterior chain, legs, shoulders, grip, core)

name: Combine Circuit
execution: Set up 4–6 simple stations and move through them in order, on your own. For a joint-friendly version, use low-impact stations — for example a loaded carry (suitcase or farmer carry), an anti-rotation core hold (Pallof press or side plank), a single-leg balance hold, a few soft-landing hops (ankle hops or stuck skater hops), and a steady bodyweight movement (squats or step-ups). Spend a set time or number of reps at each station, take a short rest as you move between them, then rest longer (1–2 minutes) after completing a full round. Complete the prescribed number of rounds. Keep the quality high at every station — this is a movement-quality circuit, not a race against the clock.
why: Combines varied movement patterns and intensities into a continuous circuit, training general work capacity, full-body conditioning, and the ability to move well across different patterns under fatigue; the variety builds broad athletic conditioning rather than a single quality.
transfer: Builds the general athletic conditioning and work capacity that support repeated efforts across a game, and the ability to perform varied movements (push, pull, sprint, jump) under fatigue — mirroring the varied physical demands of hockey.
cues: "Quality on every station" · "keep the pace, minimal rest" · "move well even when tired"
mistakes: Sacrificing form for speed; resting too long between stations; pacing too easy (no conditioning stimulus)
progression: Progress: more rounds, less rest, or harder stations | Regress: fewer rounds, more rest, or easier movements

name: Jump Rope — Steady
execution: Skip rope at a steady, sustainable pace, staying tall on the balls of the feet with small, quick hops and the wrists turning the rope (not the arms). Keep a relaxed rhythm and continuous breathing for the prescribed duration. Land softly and keep the knees and ankles springy throughout.
why: Sustained, low-to-moderate-intensity skipping develops aerobic capacity and the heart’s ability to deliver oxygen, while the repeated small hops build calf/ankle endurance, foot coordination, and reactive ankle stiffness through high-volume, low-impact contacts.
transfer: Builds the aerobic base that supports recovery between shifts and sustained work across a game, plus the calf endurance and foot/ankle coordination and stiffness that support efficient, springy skating and quick feet.
cues: "Tall, on the balls of the feet" · "turn the rope with the wrists" · "relaxed, steady rhythm"
mistakes: Big arm circles (instead of wrists); jumping too high (heavy contacts); tensing up; landing flat-footed
progression: Progress: longer duration or faster steady pace | Regress: shorter bouts or step-throughs

name: Jump Rope — Intervals
execution: Alternate harder, faster skipping bursts with easier recovery skipping (or rest) on a prescribed work-to-rest ratio — fast skipping for a set time, then easy skipping or rest, repeated. Push the pace on the work bouts and recover on the easy ones. Stay on the balls of the feet with efficient wrist turns throughout.
why: Interval skipping alternates higher-intensity efforts that tax the glycolytic and aerobic systems with recovery, training both anaerobic capacity and the aerobic system’s ability to recover between bursts; develops conditioning across intensities with low joint impact.
transfer: Mirrors the interval nature of hockey — bursts of high effort with brief recoveries; trains both the anaerobic capacity for hard bursts and the aerobic recovery between them, supporting repeated high-intensity shifts.
cues: "Fast and crisp on the work bouts" · "recover on the easy skips" · "stay light and efficient"
mistakes: Not pushing the work bouts hard enough; heavy/sloppy skipping when fatigued; inadequate recovery; big arm motions
progression: Progress: longer/harder work or shorter rest | Regress: shorter work, longer rest, or steady skipping

name: Jump Rope — Speed
execution: Perform short bursts of maximal-speed skipping — turning the rope and moving the feet as fast as possible (fast single-unders or double-unders) for a brief duration, then resting. Stay tall, light, and reactive on the balls of the feet with rapid wrist turns. Each burst is short and all-out, with full recovery between.
why: Short maximal-speed bursts train foot speed, reactive ankle stiffness, and the alactic (ATP-PC) system through brief, high-velocity efforts; the rapid contacts develop quick feet and lower-leg reactivity with full recovery preserving speed.
transfer: Builds the quick feet, rapid turnover, and reactive ankle stiffness that support fast skating strides, quick edge changes, and choppy footwork; the short maximal bursts train the speed end of foot quickness.
cues: "As fast as possible, stay light" · "rapid wrist turns" · "tall and reactive, short burst"
mistakes: Going too long (turning it into conditioning, not speed); heavy contacts; tensing the upper body; inadequate recovery
progression: Progress: double-unders or faster bursts | Regress: fast single-unders or shorter bursts

name: Tempo BW Circuit
execution: Build a simple circuit of 4–6 bodyweight exercises — for example bodyweight squats, push-ups (drop to your knees or put your hands on a bench if needed), reverse lunges, glute bridges, a plank, and easy step-ups. Do each exercise for about 30–40 seconds (or 8–12 smooth reps), then move to the next with only a short rest (about 10–20 seconds). Work at a controlled “tempo” — roughly 65–75% effort: it should feel challenging but smooth and repeatable, never all-out and never to failure. Complete the prescribed number of rounds (usually 2–3), resting 1–2 minutes between rounds. Keep every rep clean — if your form starts to break down, slow down or rest. The aim is steady, quality conditioning, not a race.
why: Moderate-intensity “tempo” work develops aerobic capacity, capillary density, and active recovery without the high stress of all-out efforts; trains the aerobic system and work capacity while promoting blood flow and recovery — a lower-stress conditioning stimulus.
transfer: Builds the aerobic base and recovery capacity that support recovering between shifts and sustaining effort across a game; the moderate, repeatable nature trains the engine that underpins repeated high-intensity work without excessive fatigue.
cues: "Smooth and controlled, not all-out" · "steady breathing" · "good form throughout"
mistakes: Going too hard (turning tempo into a max effort); sloppy form; resting too long; rushing the movements
progression: Progress: more rounds or less rest | Regress: fewer rounds, more rest, or lower intensity

name: Repeat Tempo Intervals
execution: Choose one steady, low-impact way to work — an easy-to-moderate jog, a bike, a rower, brisk incline walking, or a smooth bodyweight flow. Work for a set interval (for example 30–60 seconds) at a controlled, moderate effort of about 70% — quick enough that you feel it, but smooth enough that you could repeat it many times. Then rest for the prescribed recovery (often about equal to the work time, or a little longer) and repeat for the set number of intervals. The key is a consistent pace: every interval should look like the first — resist the urge to start fast and fade. Keep your breathing and form under control the whole way through.
why: Repeating moderate-intensity intervals with controlled rest develops aerobic capacity and the ability to sustain a strong pace repeatedly; the repeated efforts at threshold-type intensity build the aerobic engine and work capacity that support sustained and repeated efforts.
transfer: Builds the aerobic capacity and repeatable work capacity that support sustaining effort and recovering across multiple shifts and periods; trains the engine that lets a player keep producing strong efforts deep into a game.
cues: "Consistent, repeatable pace" · "don’t fade across intervals" · "controlled effort, clean form"
mistakes: Starting too fast and fading; inconsistent pacing; sloppy form; cutting recovery too short or too long
progression: Progress: more intervals, longer work, or less rest | Regress: fewer intervals, shorter work, or more rest

name: Sprint Intervals 15s
execution: Sprint maximally (running, bike, or skating-pattern work) for 15 seconds, then rest for the prescribed recovery, repeating for the set number of intervals. Push each 15-second bout near-maximally and use the recovery to partially recover before the next. Maintain effort and form across the intervals as fatigue accumulates.
why: ~15-second maximal sprints heavily tax the glycolytic system (and the tail of the alactic system), training anaerobic capacity and the ability to produce high power output repeatedly and tolerate and clear metabolic byproducts; builds the high-intensity engine for short, hard efforts.
transfer: Mirrors the duration of a hard hockey shift’s most intense bursts; trains the anaerobic capacity to produce repeated high-intensity efforts and the tolerance to keep working hard through the burn of a demanding shift.
cues: "Near-maximal each 15" · "use the rest to recover" · "hold effort across the intervals"
mistakes: Pacing instead of sprinting hard; insufficient or excessive recovery; form falling apart; fading badly across reps
progression: Progress: more intervals, shorter rest, or longer work | Regress: fewer intervals, longer rest, or shorter sprints

name: Repeat Sprint Ability
execution: Perform repeated short maximal sprints (5–10 seconds each) with short recovery between, repeating for the prescribed number. Sprint each bout at maximal effort and take only the brief prescribed rest, aiming to maintain sprint speed across all reps. The short rest is the challenge — resist the drop-off in speed.
why: Trains repeat-sprint ability — the capacity to produce maximal sprints repeatedly with incomplete recovery; this relies on the alactic system topped up by aerobic recovery and a glycolytic contribution, developing the ability to maintain power output across many short bursts with minimal rest.
transfer: Directly mirrors the repeated short, maximal bursts of a hockey shift with only brief recoveries; trains the ability to keep producing explosive skating efforts repeatedly without significant speed drop-off across a shift.
cues: "Maximal every sprint" · "short rest — minimize the drop-off" · "stay explosive, resist fatigue"
mistakes: Pacing to survive the set (not maximal); excessive speed drop-off; taking too much rest; sloppy form when tired
progression: Progress: more reps or shorter rest | Regress: fewer reps, longer rest, or longer recovery between sets

name: Aerobic Circuit (Zone 2)
execution: “Zone 2” simply means easy, steady cardio you can keep up for a long time. Pick 3–5 low-impact movements you can repeat comfortably — for example a brisk walk or easy march on the spot, an easy stationary bike or ride, light step-ups onto a low box, easy skipping rope, or gentle shadow-skating footwork — and move through them continuously for the prescribed time (usually 10–20 minutes), flowing from one to the next with little or no rest. Keep the effort easy: you should be able to hold a conversation, or breathe in and out through your nose, the entire time (about 60–70% of your maximum). If you get out of breath or have to stop, you are going too hard — slow down. Smooth, steady, and comfortable is the whole point: this builds your aerobic engine without beating up your joints.
why: Zone 2 training develops the aerobic base — increasing mitochondrial density, capillarization, and the heart’s stroke volume and ability to use fat for fuel; this low-intensity, high-volume work builds the cardiovascular engine that underpins recovery and endurance with minimal fatigue cost.
transfer: Builds the aerobic base that drives recovery between shifts and across periods — the better the aerobic engine, the faster a player recovers and the longer they sustain high-quality efforts; foundational conditioning for repeated high-intensity hockey output.
cues: "Easy, conversational pace" · "smooth and continuous" · "stay in the zone, nasal breathe"
mistakes: Drifting too high in intensity (out of Zone 2); stopping and starting; treating it as a hard workout
progression: Progress: longer duration | Regress: shorter duration or lower intensity

name: Repeat Efforts — Shift Simulation
execution: This recreates the work-then-rest rhythm of a real hockey shift, and you can do it entirely on your own. Work for about 40–60 seconds doing controlled, mixed movement — for example a few seconds of brisk skipping or marching, an easy shuttle or change of direction, then some quick (but sub-maximal) feet, and repeat — keeping everything smooth and controlled, with no maximal sprints, sharp cutting, or contact. Then “sit on the bench”: rest about 60–90 seconds, like real bench time between shifts. That is one shift. Repeat for the prescribed number of shifts. Push the work bouts to a strong but controlled effort, and use the rest to recover so every shift stays high quality rather than turning into a sloppy grind.
why: Mimics the actual work-to-rest demands of hockey shifts, taxing the glycolytic and aerobic systems in the pattern they’re used in a game; trains shift-specific conditioning — the ability to produce repeated ~40–60-second high-intensity efforts and recover between them.
transfer: Directly replicates the energy-system demands of game shifts — sustained high-intensity work with bench recovery; the most sport-specific conditioning for building the capacity to perform repeated full-intensity shifts across a game.
cues: "Work the whole shift hard" · "recover on the bench interval" · "repeat at game-like intensity"
mistakes: Pacing the shifts (not game-intensity); rest intervals too long or short; form and intensity fading across shifts
progression: Progress: more shifts, longer work, or shorter bench rest | Regress: fewer shifts, shorter work, or longer rest

name: Mirror Game / Free Play
execution: In a small space, players engage in a mirror or free-play game — mirroring a partner’s movements, playing tag, or freely moving and reacting in a competitive but unstructured way. Keep it active and reactive, changing direction and pace in response to others. Play in short, intense bouts with rest between rounds.
why: Game-based, free play trains movement, reaction, and conditioning in an unstructured, enjoyable format; the unpredictability develops open-skill agility and decision-driven movement, while the competitive context naturally raises intensity and engagement.
transfer: Mirrors the reactive, decision-rich movement of hockey — reading and reacting to others in an unstructured way; trains the open-skill agility, reaction, and competitive movement that closed drills can’t, in a fun, game-like format.
cues: "Stay active and reactive" · "read and respond to others" · "compete and have fun"
mistakes: Standing around (low engagement); not reacting (anticipating); letting it get too casual (no intensity)
progression: Progress: bigger space, more players, or add tasks | Regress: smaller space, simpler rules, or slower pace

name: Free Play / 1v1 Game
execution: Two players compete one-on-one in a small-space game — trying to reach a target, win possession of a ball/object, or beat the other to a spot — using movement, reaction, and effort to win. Play short, intense rounds with rest between, switching opponents or roles. Compete hard and react to the opponent’s actions throughout.
why: One-on-one games train reactive movement, change of direction, and effort in a directly competitive context; the live opponent forces real-time reading and reacting, building open-skill agility and the competitive drive and conditioning of head-to-head battles.
transfer: Mirrors the one-on-one battles of hockey — beating an opponent to a puck or spot, winning a race, or competing for position; trains the reaction, agility, and compete level used in the countless 1v1 situations of a game.
cues: "Compete to win" · "react to your opponent, not the fake" · "stay low and ready"
mistakes: Low compete level; anticipating instead of reacting; standing tall; over-committing to fakes
progression: Progress: more space, harder constraints, or add a puck | Regress: smaller space or simpler win conditions

name: Battle Game / 1v1
execution: Two players engage in a 1v1 battle for possession or position — protecting an object/ball while the other tries to win it, or competing for a spot using body position and leverage. Use a wide base, low center of gravity, and body positioning to win or hold possession. Battle hard in short rounds with rest, then switch.
why: Battle games train the body-positioning, leverage, anti-rotation core stiffness, and lower-body strength used to win physical contests; competing for position against a live opponent develops strength-in-contact and compete level in a realistic, resisted context.
transfer: Directly mirrors hockey board and net-front battles — protecting the puck, winning body position, and using leverage and a strong base against an opponent; trains the contact strength, core stiffness, and compete level central to winning puck battles.
cues: "Wide base, stay low" · "use leverage and body position" · "compete hard, protect possession"
mistakes: Standing too tall (losing leverage); a narrow base (off-balance); reaching instead of using the body; low compete
progression: Progress: stronger opponent or harder constraints | Regress: lighter contact or a simpler battle
muscles: Glutes, legs, core, full body (contact strength)

name: Free Play with Intent
execution: Engage in free, game-like play but with a specific intent or constraint emphasized by the coach — focusing on quick first steps, staying low, reacting fast, or using a particular movement. Play freely and competitively while consciously applying the targeted quality throughout the bout. Short, intense rounds with rest.
why: Adds a purposeful constraint or focus to free play, channeling the enjoyment and unpredictability of games toward developing a specific quality; the constraint-led approach lets a targeted skill (e.g., quick acceleration or low posture) be trained within realistic, reactive game movement.
transfer: Mirrors the reactive movement of hockey while reinforcing a specific quality — quick first steps, low athletic posture, or fast reactions — in a game context; trains the targeted skill in the open, decision-rich environment where it’s actually used.
cues: "Play free, but apply the focus" · "keep the intent every rep" · "compete and react"
mistakes: Losing the intended focus once play gets competitive; low engagement; the constraint being too restrictive (killing the flow)
progression: Progress: combine multiple intents or add complexity | Regress: a single simple focus or slower pace

name: Slow Walk with Nose Breathing
execution: Walk slowly and easily for the prescribed duration, breathing only through the nose — slow, deep, controlled inhales and exhales. Keep the pace gentle and the body relaxed, letting the heart rate gradually come down. Focus on the calm, rhythmic nasal breathing throughout the walk.
why: A slow walk with nasal breathing promotes parasympathetic (“rest and digest”) activation, helping downregulate the nervous system after training, lower the heart rate, and begin recovery; nasal breathing encourages slower, fuller breaths that aid relaxation and recovery.
transfer: Supports recovery between sessions and downregulation after intense work — restoring the calm state that aids adaptation and readiness; the recovery focus, rather than performance, helps the body bounce back for the next training or game.
cues: "Slow, easy pace" · "breathe only through the nose" · "relax and let the heart rate drop"
mistakes: Walking too briskly; mouth breathing; rushing; staying tense
progression: Progress: longer duration or add breath-hold practice | Regress: shorter duration

name: Child's Pose with Breath
execution: Kneel and sit the hips back toward the heels, reaching the arms forward and lowering the chest toward the floor, forehead resting down. Relax into the position and breathe slowly and deeply, feeling the back and hips gently open with each exhale. Hold for the prescribed time, breathing calmly throughout.
why: A gentle, restful position that lightly stretches the lower back, hips, and lats while the focused breathing promotes relaxation and parasympathetic activation; combines mild mobility with a calming, recovery-oriented breathing focus.
transfer: Aids recovery by gently decompressing the spine, opening the hips, and relaxing the nervous system after training; supports the relaxation and mobility that help the body recover and stay supple for skating.
cues: "Sit the hips back to the heels" · "breathe slow and deep" · "relax and soften with each exhale"
mistakes: Holding tension; shallow breathing; forcing the stretch; rushing
progression: Progress: walk the hands to one side for a lat stretch | Regress: place a cushion under the hips for comfort

name: Legs Up the Wall (or Shin Pull)
execution: Lie on your back with the hips near a wall and the legs extended up against it, arms relaxed at the sides. Let the legs rest supported by the wall and breathe slowly and deeply, relaxing fully. Hold for the prescribed time. (Alternatively, gently pull a shin toward the chest for a light hip stretch.) Keep the whole body relaxed.
why: Elevating the legs aids venous return and circulation while the supported, restful position and slow breathing promote parasympathetic relaxation; a low-effort recovery posture that helps drain the legs, reduce fatigue sensation, and calm the nervous system.
transfer: Supports lower-body recovery after the heavy leg demands of skating and training — aiding circulation and relaxation to help the legs recover and feel fresher; a restorative posture that aids between-session recovery.
cues: "Let the wall support the legs" · "breathe slow, fully relax" · "soften the whole body"
mistakes: Tensing the legs; shallow breathing; staying for too short a time to relax
progression: Progress: longer duration or add gentle ankle pumps | Regress: legs on a chair instead of the wall

name: Figure-4 Stretch
execution: Lie on your back, cross one ankle over the opposite thigh (forming a “4”), then reach through and gently pull the supporting thigh toward the chest until you feel a stretch in the crossed-leg glute/hip. Keep the head and shoulders relaxed on the floor and breathe slowly. Hold for the prescribed time, then switch sides.
why: Stretches the glutes and deep hip rotators (including the piriformis) in a supported, relaxed position; the gentle, breath-paced hold improves hip mobility and releases tension in the posterior hip — a commonly tight area for athletes.
transfer: Restores the glute and deep-hip-rotator mobility that supports hip range for skating, crossovers, and turns; releasing posterior-hip tension helps maintain the hip mobility and comfort that support efficient skating mechanics.
cues: "Make a figure-4, pull the thigh in" · "relax the head and shoulders" · "breathe into the hip"
mistakes: Forcing the pull; lifting the head/tensing; holding the breath; bouncing
progression: Progress: pull closer or do it seated/standing for more load | Regress: smaller range or support the head

name: Pigeon Stretch
execution: From a kneeling or all-fours position, bring one shin forward across the body and extend the other leg straight back, lowering the hips toward the floor. Keep the hips square and fold the torso forward over the front shin to deepen the front-hip/glute stretch. Breathe slowly and hold, then switch sides. Support with the hands as needed.
why: A deep stretch for the front-leg glute and external rotators and the rear-leg hip flexors; the supported fold and relaxed breathing improve deep hip mobility in two directions at once, addressing the tightness that accumulates in the hips from training and sport.
transfer: Restores the deep hip mobility (rotation and flexion/extension) used in the wide skating stance, crossovers, and stride; maintaining this range supports stride depth and reduces hip stiffness that can limit skating mechanics.
cues: "Hips square, fold forward" · "breathe into the front hip" · "ease into it, no forcing"
mistakes: Letting the hips rotate or collapse to one side; forcing the depth; holding the breath; knee discomfort (adjust the angle)
progression: Progress: fold deeper or hold longer | Regress: elevate the hip on a cushion or do a figure-4 instead
muscles: N/A (mobility/recovery — glutes, hip rotators, hip flexors)

name: Cat-Cow
execution: On hands and knees, slowly alternate between rounding the spine toward the ceiling (cat — tucking the chin and pelvis) and arching it down (cow — lifting the chest and tailbone). Move smoothly with the breath — exhale into the cat, inhale into the cow — flowing through a comfortable range. Repeat for the prescribed reps.
why: A gentle, breath-paced spinal flow that mobilizes the spine through flexion and extension, lubricating the segments and relaxing the back muscles; the rhythmic, breath-linked movement promotes spinal mobility and a calming, recovery-oriented stimulus.
transfer: Restores spinal mobility and relaxes the back after the loading of training and the flexed posture of skating; maintaining segmental spinal movement supports a healthy, mobile back and comfortable skating posture.
cues: "Round into the cat, arch into the cow" · "move with the breath" · "smooth and controlled, comfortable range"
mistakes: Forcing the end ranges; moving too fast (not with the breath); only moving from the low back (move the whole spine)
progression: Progress: add gentle side-bends or segmental focus | Regress: smaller range or slower tempo

name: Supine Spinal Twist
execution: Lie on your back, draw one knee up and across the body toward the floor on the opposite side, extending the same-side arm out and turning the head the other way. Keep the shoulders relaxed toward the floor and breathe slowly, letting the spine and hip gently rotate. Hold for the prescribed time, then switch sides.
why: A gentle rotational stretch for the spine, glutes, and chest; the supported, relaxed twist with slow breathing improves rotary spinal mobility and releases tension along the back and hips, in a low-effort recovery posture.
transfer: Restores the rotational mobility of the spine and hips used in shooting, passing, and turning, and releases tension that accumulates from training; maintaining rotary mobility supports the trunk rotation behind shots and comfortable skating.
cues: "Knee across, arm out, look away" · "shoulders relaxed to the floor" · "breathe into the twist, no force"
mistakes: Forcing the knee down; tensing the shoulders up; holding the breath; rushing
progression: Progress: deeper twist or longer hold | Regress: place a cushion under the knee or reduce range

name: Hip / Groin Flow
execution: Move through a flowing sequence of hip and groin mobility movements — deep squat holds, adductor rockers, hip circles, and gentle lunges with rotation — transitioning smoothly between positions and breathing throughout. Move slowly and rhythmically, easing into each range without forcing. Complete the prescribed flow.
why: A flowing mobility sequence gently takes the hips and groin through multiple ranges, maintaining and restoring the hip and adductor mobility that the wide demands of skating require; the flowing, breath-paced format promotes mobility and recovery in the most skating-relevant areas.
transfer: Restores and maintains the hip and groin mobility central to the wide skating stance, crossovers, and stride; keeping these areas mobile supports stride range and is a key strategy to reduce the groin/hip strains common in hockey.
cues: "Flow smoothly between positions" · "breathe and ease into each range" · "no forcing, move with control"
mistakes: Forcing ranges; rushing the flow; holding the breath; skipping the groin-specific positions
progression: Progress: deeper ranges or longer holds in each position | Regress: smaller ranges or fewer positions

name: 20m Sprint
execution: From a stationary two-point stance, sprint a flat-out 20 metres in a straight line. Drive hard out of the start with a forward lean and powerful arm action, staying low for the first strides, then rise gradually as you build speed. Run through the 20-metre line without decelerating. Time each effort, taking full recovery between reps on the same surface and footwear.
why: Trains and measures pure acceleration — the ability to overcome inertia and apply large horizontal forces over the first 20 metres. Short-distance sprinting develops the explosive force production and powerful arm-leg coordination that a longer run rarely taxes.
transfer: Almost every sprint in hockey is short and acceleration-dominant — jumping on a loose puck, beating an opponent to the boards, exploding out on a breakaway. A faster 20-metre time is a direct dry-land read on first-step quickness.
cues: "Push the ground back, don’t reach" · "lean and drive the arms" · "low and patient, then tall"
mistakes: Popping upright on the first steps; over-striding instead of pushing; tensing the shoulders and face; easing off before the line
progression: Progress: resisted starts (sled or band) or extend to a 30 m sprint | Regress: 10 m accelerations focused on the drive phase

name: 20m Flying Sprint
execution: Build speed gradually over a 20–30 metre run-in, then hit a flat-out, maximal-velocity 20-metre flying zone. Run tall and relaxed with a fast, cyclical leg action and brief ground contacts — the goal is the highest speed you can hold through the zone, not acceleration. Time only the flying 20 metres, with full recovery between efforts.
why: Isolates maximal sprinting velocity by removing the acceleration phase, so you train and measure pure top-end speed and the efficient, relaxed mechanics that let an athlete hold it. Flying sprints expose and develop the highest-velocity stride a player can produce.
transfer: Top-end speed separates players on long, straight-line efforts — beating a defender wide, backchecking to erase a rush, or stretching the ice. Training high-velocity mechanics also builds the hamstring resilience those speeds demand.
cues: "Tall and relaxed — float, don’t strain" · "strike down and back, quick off the ground" · "fast hands, loose face"
mistakes: Tensing up and over-striding; reaching the feet out in front of the body; trying to keep accelerating through the zone instead of holding speed; entering the zone unrecovered
progression: Progress: lengthen the fly zone or add light assisted (downhill / towed) sprints | Regress: shorten to a 10 m fly or run build-up strides

name: Beep Test
execution: Set two markers exactly 20 metres apart on a flat, non-slip surface and play the standard beep-test audio (free "beep test" or "multistage fitness test" apps and tracks are widely available). Run from one line to the other, reaching the far line before each beep, then turn and run back on the next beep. The beeps start slow and speed up at the end of every level, so you run faster and faster. Keep going as long as you can reach the line in time; your score is the level and shuttle you reach when you can no longer keep pace (or choose to stop). Warm up thoroughly first, ease into the early levels, and STOP at any sharp or joint pain — this is a hard, maximal test, so respect it and push only as hard as your body allows.
why: The beep test is a simple, repeatable field measure of maximal aerobic capacity (VO2max). By making you run progressively faster until you cannot keep up, it puts one honest number on the size of your aerobic engine — the system that powers recovery between shifts and across a game — so you can track whether it grows over the eight weeks.
transfer: Your aerobic engine is what lets you recover between shifts and still skate hard in the third period. A higher beep-test level means faster between-shift recovery and more high-quality shifts in a game — the difference between fading late and finishing strong.
cues: Reach the line before the beep; turn tight and push off; ease in and build; stop on sharp pain
mistakes: Starting too fast and burning out early; not reaching the line before the beep; testing cold; pushing through joint pain on the turns
progression: Progression: a higher level or more shuttles. Regression: stop earlier, or use a longer shuttle (about 30 m) with gentler turns if the sharp 180-degree turns bother your knees or ankles.

name: Groin Adductor Slide
execution: Stand on a smooth floor in socks, or use a slide board. Place one foot on a slider or towel. Start with feet together. Slowly slide the foot outward — controlled by the adductor of that leg. Go as wide as comfortable, feeling the groin stretch under load. Pull the foot back in using the adductor — the concentric return. Complete 8-10 reps each side. Control every centimetre of the slide.
why: The groin adductor slide eccentrically loads the adductors through the exact skating stride range — it is the most direct off-ice translation of the groin's role in controlling the stride width and generating medial force. Regular eccentric adductor work has been shown to increase adductor tendon cross-sectional area, making the tendon more resistant to the repetitive strain that causes chronic groin problems in skaters.
transfer: Active groin mobility — replaces the passive stretch with dynamic control. Pair with Copenhagen plank for full adductor coverage: stretch + strength = injury-proof groin.
cues: "Wide stance" · "Shift weight to one side" · "Lower into a side lunge" · "Slide foot out"
mistakes: Sliding too fast — the entire value is in the slow, resisted control. Going beyond comfortable range before you have the strength — build range gradually over weeks. Only sliding one direction — equally important to train the non-dominant side. Skipping it because it feels fine — groin injuries don't announce themselves before they happen.
progression: Progress: Lateral lunge to slider — combines bodyweight load with the adductor slide demand. | Regress: Seated butterfly with gentle knee press — passive adductor stretch to begin restoring range.

name: Inchworm Walk
execution: Stand tall, feet hip-width apart. Hinge forward at the hips — KEEP LEGS AS STRAIGHT AS POSSIBLE — and place hands on the floor. Walk the hands forward until you're in a high plank position. Hold the plank 1-2 seconds — chest stable, hips level, core tight. Walk the feet UP to the hands in small steps — legs stay as straight as the hamstrings allow. Stand up. That's one rep. 5-10 reps.
why: The inchworm walk combines three full-body qualities in one move: posterior-chain mobility (hamstring stretch when walking feet to hands), core control + shoulder stability (the plank position), and full-body coordination. For hockey players whose hamstrings are chronically tight from the skating stride, this is one of the few warm-up movements that simultaneously LOADS the hamstrings while stretching them — mobility through strength. It's the single best general warm-up before a leg-day session.
transfer: Full-body mobility + core control + shoulder stability in one move. Loosens tight hamstrings (the #1 hockey limitation) while building the plank position used in skating mechanics. Daily warm-up forever. Three minutes of inchworms beats 10 minutes of static stretching.
cues: "Stand tall. Hinge forward" · "Walk hands out on the floor until you're in a high plank. Hold 1 second. Walk feet UP to your hands (keep legs as straight as possible). Stand up. Repeat."
mistakes: Bending the knees on the walk-in — defeats the hamstring stretch. Keep legs as straight as your mobility allows. Letting hips sag in the plank — wasted core opportunity. Brace it. Rushing the walks — slow and controlled, especially on the feet-walk-in phase. Skipping the plank pause — that's where the shoulder and core stability lives.
progression: Progress: Inchworm + push-up — add 1 push-up at the plank phase. Doubles as upper-body activation. | Regress: Short inchworm (walk hands out only halfway, not all the way to plank) — same pattern, less ROM demand.

name: Barbell Back Squat
execution: Set the bar at upper-back height in a power rack. Step under, bar across upper traps (high bar) or rear delts (low bar). Brace abs HARD, take a tight grip outside shoulders. Step back 2-3 paces with feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out. Initiate the descent by sitting hips back AND breaking at knees simultaneously. Descend until hip crease is below knee — 'parallel'. Knees track over toes. Drive back up by pushing the floor away — chest stays up, no forward dump. Lock out fully at top with hips and knees extended.
why: The back squat is the single most-studied lower-body strength builder. For hockey, it develops the quad/glute/hamstring chain that produces every skating stride. Athletes with a back squat ≥ 1.6× bodyweight outperform weaker athletes in skating speed by 12-15%. The depth and load capacity also build the connective tissue resilience required for in-season durability.
transfer: Foundation of lower body strength — drives skating power. Three reps at 85%, four sets, three minutes rest. The hockey-specific max strength prescription. No shortcuts.
cues: "Chest up" · "Knees track toes" · "Break parallel" · "Drive through heels"
mistakes: Knees collapsing inward (valgus) — major injury risk. Cue 'spread the floor'. Heels coming up — usually ankle mobility issue. Use 5-10mm lifters or work ankle mobility. Forward dump (chest collapses) — usually weak upper back. Slow the eccentric, fix by adding rows. Cutting depth — limits glute/hamstring recruitment. Better to drop the weight and squat full range.
progression: Progress: Pause squat (3-second pause at depth) once form is dialed. Builds bottom-position strength for skating starts. | Regress: Goblet squat with kettlebell. Easier to keep upright posture, builds the pattern with less spinal load.

name: Calf Raise Iso Hold
execution: Stand with the balls of your feet on the edge of a step (or on flat floor). Push to the very top of a calf raise — heels as high as they go. HOLD. Weight stays on the balls of the feet, ankles fully extended, knees soft. Single-leg version: same setup, one foot only (other foot lifted off). Hold steady — no bouncing or dropping mid-hold. Lower under control. Repeat or switch.
why: Ankle stiffness — the foot's ability to act like a spring rather than a soft pad on push-off — is one of the most under-trained qualities in hockey training, and it's directly tied to skating speed. Each stride, the foot transfers energy from leg drive into ice push, and that transfer is lossy if the ankle is sloppy. Holding the top of a calf raise builds soleus and gastrocnemius isometric strength — the muscles that lock the ankle into rigid spring mode. The bonus: same muscles that protect against Achilles strains and shin-splint pain. Cheap to do, high carryover, almost no one trains it. Easy win.
transfer: Ankle stiffness is the most under-trained quality in skating — it determines how much of your leg drive actually transfers into ice push. Iso-holding the top of a calf raise builds it directly. Drop to single-leg as soon as two-foot is easy — same muscle, way more load.
cues: "Stand on the edge of a step (or flat floor). Push to the very top of a calf raise — heels as high as they go. HOLD. Two-foot for beginner" · "Single-leg for advanced."
mistakes: Rocking outward onto the pinky-toe edge of the foot — keep weight on the big toe through to the second-toe ball. Bending the knees to cheat the top — knees stay soft but extended. Bouncing in and out of the hold — defeats the iso; one continuous push to the top. Going single-leg before bilateral is bombproof — earn 45-60s solid two-foot first.
progression: Progress: Single-leg calf raise iso hold. Or weighted (dumbbell in hand, kettlebell racked). | Regress: Bilateral on flat floor (no step edge) — shorter range, same iso quality.

name: Front Squat
execution: Set the bar in the front rack position — resting on the front deltoids, elbows HIGH and forward. Feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out. Keep elbows high throughout — if they drop the bar rolls forward. Sit DOWN between the knees — more vertical torso than a back squat. Descend until hip crease is below the knee. Knees track over toes. Drive the floor away to stand — chest up, elbows stay high.
why: The front squat demands a more upright torso than the back squat, which better replicates the skating position — knees forward, hips loaded, spine tall. It develops quad dominance while requiring serious upper-back and core strength to hold the bar. For hockey players it is an excellent tool for building knee strength and the forward-lean positioning used in the skating crouch.
transfer: Builds quad strength and upright posture — mimics skating stance. Goalies live in this position. If you play goalie, front squat is non-negotiable.
cues: "Elbows high" · "Keep bar on front delts" · "Stay upright" · "Deep squat"
mistakes: Elbows dropping — kills the front rack and dumps the bar forward. Elbows up, always. Heels coming up — ankle mobility issue. Work dorsiflexion or use small heel lift temporarily. Leaning forward — front squat requires more upright torso than back squat. If you lean, the load is too heavy. Wrist pain in the rack position — work wrist flexibility or use a cross-arm grip temporarily.
progression: Progress: Pause front squat (3s at the bottom) — builds bottom-position strength for low skating stance. | Regress: Goblet squat — same upright torso demand with much easier load management.

name: Hang Power Clean
execution: Start with the bar hanging at hip/thigh level — knees slightly bent, hips back. This is the 'hang' position: flat back, bar touching thighs, weight on mid-foot. Initiate by driving the hips FORWARD explosively — the hip snap drives the bar upward. As the bar rises, shrug the traps aggressively, then pull the elbows HIGH and outside. Drop under the bar quickly — rotating elbows forward to catch in the front rack. Catch with knees slightly bent. Stand tall. Lower the bar to hang. Repeat.
why: The hang power clean is the most complete athletic power exercise — it trains triple extension (ankle, knee, hip) at maximum velocity plus the rapid descent under the bar (catching phase), which builds the reactive strength pattern of absorbing and redirecting force on the ice. Many NHL teams use the power clean as their primary power development tool precisely because it trains the entire kinetic chain simultaneously.
transfer: Trains explosive triple extension (ankle/knee/hip) under load — the exact pattern of a skating stride. Builds rate of force development. Requires coaching — if you have not been taught the catch position, substitute trap-bar jump or hang clean PULL (no-catch variant). Triphasic Phase 2 (max power). The bridge between heavy strength and plyometrics. Best of both worlds.
cues: "Bar at hip" · "Hinge to mid-thigh" · "Explode hips through" · "Shrug hard" · "Catch in quarter squat. Speed > weight. If the catch is shaky" · "Stop — drop to a clean pull (no catch) until coached."
mistakes: Pulling with the arms too early — the arms just guide the bar. Power comes from the hip drive. Bar drifting away from the body — keep it close throughout the pull. Catching with a stiff lower body — the catch requires a quarter squat to absorb. Ego loading — technique falls apart above a certain weight. Keep it clean.
progression: Progress: Full power clean from the floor — adds a more challenging starting position. | Regress: Kettlebell swing — same hip drive mechanics without the catch complexity.

name: Hip Airplane Hold
execution: Stand on one leg. Standing knee can be slightly soft (not locked, not bent). Hinge at the hip — torso drops forward, back leg lifts behind you. Continue until torso and back leg form a straight line parallel to the floor (a 'T' from the side). Arms extend out wide to the sides for balance. Square the hips — point both hip bones at the floor (don't let the back-leg hip rotate open). HOLD. Standing leg solid, no twisting. Stand under control. Switch.
why: The hip airplane is the deep-stabilizer test most off-ice training programs miss. Holding a single-leg T-position — torso and back leg parallel to the floor, hips square — recruits the glute medius, deep hip rotators, and posterior-chain stabilizers that control hip rotation under load. For hockey, that's the EXACT muscle system that keeps a skate edge tracking through a tight turn: when an athlete's outside hip rotates uncontrolled, they lose the edge. Adding 15-25s isometric holds in this position builds the rotational stability that pays off in cleaner turns, better balance through contact, and dramatically lower rates of nagging hip and groin issues across a season.
transfer: Single-leg balance plus hip-rotation control under hold — the same deep stabilizer system that keeps a skate edge tracking through tight turns. Most overlooked iso in hockey training. Catching yourself with the back leg means the hold is lost. End the set there — quality over time.
cues: "Single-leg stance. Hinge at the hip — torso and back leg form a straight "T" parallel to the floor. Arms out wide. HOLD without letting the hip drop or rotate. Switch legs."
mistakes: Back-leg hip rotating open (turning sideways) — kills the whole point; force both hip bones to point down. Standing knee locking out fully — keep it soft so the hip muscles work, not the joint. Catching with the back foot when balance fails — once that happens, end the set; the hold is over. Arching the lower back — torso stays straight, like a board parallel to the floor.
progression: Progress: Eyes closed (removes visual balance feedback — makes it ~30% harder). Or hold a light dumbbell in the lifted arm. | Regress: Hand on a wall or pole for balance — same T position, less stability demand.
muscles: Glute medius, Hip stabilizers, Hamstrings, Core

name: Leg Extension (Machine)
execution: Sit on the leg extension machine. Pad sits just above the ankles. Grip the handles for stability. Back flat against the pad. Extend both legs smoothly to full lockout — quads fully contracted. Pause 1-2 seconds at full extension — this is where VMO fires hardest. Lower slowly — 3 seconds — back to the start position. Do not swing the torso to help the lift.',.
why: The leg extension isolates the quadriceps in open-chain knee extension — building the VMO (inner quad) strength that stabilises the patella tracking and prevents 'runner's knee', which is common in hockey players from heavy skating volume. While not a sport-specific movement, it is an important accessory exercise for correcting quad development gaps and supporting knee joint health.
transfer: Isolates quads — builds terminal knee extension strength for skating. Don't do leg extensions on heavy squat day. Pick one heavy quad stimulus per session — they don't add, they redundancy.
cues: "Full range of motion" · "Squeeze at top" · "Slow lowering"
mistakes: Partial range — full extension is required for VMO activation. Fast lowering — the slow eccentric builds the patella-stabilising strength. Too heavy — should be able to do full range with smooth control.',. Using this as a substitute for squats — it supplements, never replaces, compound work.',.
progression: Progress: Single-leg extension — identifies and corrects left-right quad imbalances. | Regress: Terminal knee extension (TKE) with band — lighter, safer, great VMO activation.',

name: Leg Press
execution: Sit in the leg press. Feet shoulder-width on the platform, mid-height. Unrack the weight. Lower the platform by bending the knees. Descend until knees reach 90° — thighs parallel to the platform. Drive through the full foot — not just the toes — to press back to start. Do NOT lock the knees out explosively — stop just short of full lock.',. Keep the lower back flat against the pad throughout.',.
why: The leg press allows higher absolute loads than the squat with significantly less spinal compression — making it ideal for developing pure quad and glute strength in players with lower-back limitations or during high-volume phases when spinal fatigue is a concern. Sled-press force output correlates well with skating acceleration, and the machine's guided path allows full attention on maximal force production.
transfer: Safe way to load leg strength without spinal compression. Leg press is supplemental, not primary. Heavy squats remain king. Use leg press to add volume without CNS cost.
cues: "Feet shoulder-width" · "Lower to 90°" · "Press through heels" · "Do not lock knees"
mistakes: Feet too low — increases knee stress. Mid-platform is neutral.',. Lower back peeling off the seat at the bottom — reduce the range of motion.',. Locking out the knees with a jolt — controlled extension only.',. Using the leg press as a squat replacement entirely — it doesn't train stabilisers.',.
progression: Progress: Single-leg press — unilateral loading corrects imbalances and increases demand.', | Regress: Bodyweight squat — learn the pattern before adding any external load.',

name: Pause Squat
execution: Set up exactly as a back squat — bar on upper back, feet shoulder-width. Descend under full control to the bottom position (hip crease below knee). STOP completely — eliminate all bounce. Pause for 3 full seconds. During the pause: stay braced, knees out, chest up. Do not relax. Drive back to the top — this is harder than any regular squat. Breathe at the top between reps. Don't rush.
why: The pause squat (3-5 second hold at the bottom) eliminates the stretch-reflex bounce that most athletes rely on, forcing the muscles to produce force from a dead stop — identical to the demand of a skating start from a stationary position. It builds the bottom-position quad and glute strength that is significantly undertrained in normal squatting and directly improves first-step quickness from a standstill.
transfer: Eliminates the bounce — trains true strength from a dead stop. Three reps × four sets at 70%. Pause squats teach patience. Pause squats also expose every weakness in the bottom position.
cues: "Squat to parallel" · "Pause 3 seconds" · "No bounce" · "Drive explosively up"
mistakes: Bouncing even slightly out of the hole — any bounce defeats the purpose. Relaxing the core during the pause — stay fully braced throughout. Too heavy — pause squats require 10-20% less load than regular squats. Short pause — 3 seconds minimum. Count it out loud if needed.
progression: Progress: Tempo squat (5s down, 3s pause, explosive up) — adds eccentric control to the pause. | Regress: Goblet squat with pause — lighter load, easier to maintain upright torso.

name: Spanish Squat (Isometric)
execution: Anchor a heavy resistance band around a sturdy upright at knee height. Step inside the band so it wraps around the back of both knees. Walk backward until the band is taut and actively pulling you forward. Sit back into a quarter-to-half squat — torso tall and vertical (this is the giveaway: no forward lean). Knees stay tracking over the toes; resist the band's forward pull. HOLD. Hold until quads burn out. Step forward to release.
why: The Spanish squat is the gold-standard isometric for the patellar tendon — the structure that takes the brunt of every stop, every crossover acceleration, and every change of direction a skater performs. Anchoring a heavy band around the back of the knees creates a horizontal pulling force that has to be resisted by quad isometric contraction, loading the tendon directly without the spinal compression of a back squat. Sports-medicine clinics use this as the FIRST-line protocol for jumper's knee (patellar tendinopathy) — both for treatment and prevention. Hockey players who add 2 × 30-60s of Spanish squats per week experience dramatically lower rates of nagging anterior knee pain across a season.
transfer: The gold-standard patellar tendon isometric — bulletproofs the knees against the constant stop-start loading of skating. Sports medicine's primary protocol for jumper's-knee prevention and rehab. Make the band heavy enough that it actively pulls — if you're not resisting, the iso isn't there. Add band tension before adding time.
cues: "Heavy band anchored at knee-height around a sturdy post. Step inside so it wraps the back of both knees. Sit back into a quarter-to-half squat — band pulls forward" · "You resist. Torso tall. HOLD."
mistakes: Leaning forward at the hips — converts it into a regular squat and unloads the patellar tendon. Band too light — if you're not actively pulling against it, the iso stimulus isn't there. Use the heaviest band that lets you hold for ≥30s. Knees caving inward — push out against the band actively. Going too deep (full squat) — quarter-to-half is the working range; deeper makes it a leg workout, not a tendon iso.
progression: Progress: Heavier band + longer hold (60-90s). Or single-leg Spanish squat with band on one knee only. | Regress: Lighter band + shallower depth (quarter-squat only). Or bodyweight wall sit while you build base quad endurance.

name: Standing Calf Raise (DBs)
execution: Stand on the edge of a step or plate — heels hanging off the edge. Lower heels as far below the step as possible — full stretch at the bottom. Push up onto the balls of your feet as high as possible — full contraction at top. Pause 1 second at the top. Lower for 3 seconds. Keep knees straight for gastrocnemius; slightly bent for soleus. Use one leg at a time for maximum loading.
why: The calf (gastrocnemius + soleus) is the primary ankle plantar flexor — it provides the final snap in each skating stride and generates the spring energy through the Achilles tendon. Weak calves are a direct brake on stride frequency and power. They are also the first line of defense against Achilles tendinopathy, which is chronically undertrained in hockey players who rely entirely on skating for lower-leg development.
transfer: Builds calf strength for explosive push-off and skating acceleration. Add tempo: 3 seconds down, 1 second hold at top. Tempo work is where calves actually grow.
cues: "Full range of motion" · "Pause at top" · "Slow lower" · "Use full heel drop"
mistakes: Partial range — bounce-style reps with no stretch. Full range only. Both legs always — single-leg is where real strength lives. Skipping the slow eccentric — Achilles injury prevention requires eccentric loading. Treating calves as an afterthought — 3 sets twice a week is enough to make a real difference.
progression: Progress: Single-leg weighted calf raise (hold dumbbell) — dramatically increases load. | Regress: Double-leg calf raise with bodyweight — build the pattern before going single-leg.

name: Tempo Squat (3-1-1)
execution: Set up for a back squat — bar on upper back, feet shoulder-width. Lower over 3-5 seconds — count it out. Controlled, not grinding. Pause 2-3 seconds at the bottom — no bounce, stay tight. Drive back up as EXPLOSIVELY as possible — maximum intent on the concentric. The contrast between slow descent and explosive ascent is the stimulus. Rest fully between reps at the top.
why: The tempo squat (slow eccentric + pause + explosive concentric) develops all three components of the strength-speed curve simultaneously. The slow eccentric (3-5 seconds) builds quad and glute time-under-tension; the pause eliminates the stretch reflex; the explosive concentric trains rate of force development. For hockey players, this combination directly improves the first-step explosiveness that comes after absorbing a hockey stop.
transfer: Builds hypertrophy and connective tissue strength with time under tension. Three sets × 8 with controlled tempo. Goblet or front loading is ideal — back squat tempo is brutal on the spine.
cues: "3 seconds down" · "1 second pause" · "1 second up — controlled throughout"
mistakes: Relaxing at the bottom — stay fully braced during the pause. Explosive on the way down too — only the eccentric is slow. Not the concentric. Too heavy — tempo squats require 15-20% less load than regular squats. Rushing the eccentric — count it out loud if needed.
progression: Progress: Longer eccentric (5-6 seconds) or longer pause (4-5 seconds) as you adapt. | Regress: Goblet squat with 2s pause — same concept with a lighter, more forgiving implement.

name: Barbell Hip Thrust
execution: Sit on the floor with upper back against a sturdy bench, knees bent, feet flat. Roll a loaded barbell over your hips. Use a barbell pad — do NOT skip this. Drive feet through the floor, extend hips upward. Squeeze glutes HARD at the top. Ribs DOWN, chin tucked — don't hyperextend the lower back to fake range of motion. Pause 1-2 seconds at the top. This is where 80% of the glute work happens. Lower under control, don't crash the bar to the floor.
why: The barbell hip thrust isolates the glutes with the bar's resistance vector horizontal — exactly the direction of force production in skating push-off. It produces roughly 3× higher glute activation than back squats at equivalent loads. For hockey players, strong glutes mean better stride length and reduced knee/lower-back injury risk.
transfer: Directly trains glute extension — the primary muscle in skating push-off. Most hockey players are quad-dominant. Hip thrusts are how you flip that. Train the glutes, train the skating.
cues: "Upper back on bench" · "Bar on hips" · "Drive through heels" · "Squeeze glutes at top"
mistakes: Hyperextending the lower back to fake higher hips — defeats the exercise. Ribs DOWN. Feet too close — converts it to a quad exercise. Heels should be ~12-18 inches from glutes at top. Pushing through toes — should feel mid-foot/heel pressure for glute engagement. No pad on the bar — stops you from using meaningful loads. Get the pad.
progression: Progress: Single-leg hip thrust (foot elevated on bench) — highest hockey transfer due to unilateral loading. | Regress: Bodyweight glute bridge first. Learn the squeeze pattern before loading the bar.

name: Conventional Deadlift
execution: Stand with feet hip-width, bar over mid-foot (1 inch from shins). Hinge at the hips and grip the bar — double overhand or mixed grip. Set the back: chest tall, lats engaged, bar close to shins. Big breath into the belly, brace the core 360°. Push the floor away — leg drive first, then hips and back rise together. Bar stays in contact with the legs the entire way up. Stand fully tall — hips locked, shoulders back. Lower with control.
why: The conventional deadlift is the king of posterior chain development — glutes, hamstrings, spinal erectors, and traps all working together to lift maximal load from the floor. For hockey players, it builds the raw pulling and hip-hinge strength that underpins skating power, board battles, and spinal resilience. NHL strength coaches use deadlift strength (relative to bodyweight) as a primary indicator of an athlete's physical readiness.
transfer: Full-body strength king — builds power from the floor up. Three rep sets at 80-85%. Conventional is taxing — three working sets is plenty. Quality > volume.
cues: "Bar over laces" · "Big breath brace core" · "Push floor away" · "Hips and shoulders rise together"
mistakes: Bar drifting away from the body — drags the bar back in close. Treat it like a leg press. Jerking the bar off the floor — take the slack out first, then apply steady force. Rounding the lower back — set the brace before pulling. No exceptions. Hyperextending at the top — stand neutral, not leaned back.
progression: Progress: Deficit deadlift (stand on 2-inch plates) — increases ROM and starting position difficulty. | Regress: Trap bar deadlift — same hip hinge, more upright torso, less technical demand.

name: Hamstring Walkout
execution: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat on the floor. Drive hips up into a bridge position — same as a glute bridge. From the top, walk both feet forward — sliding the heels away from your body. Walk as far as you can while keeping the hips elevated and the back flat. Once at maximum extension, walk back in to the start. Keep the hips up the entire time — they must not sag.
why: The hamstring walkout eccentrically loads the hamstrings through their full length — from the hip to the knee — which is the exact injury mechanism of a hamstring strain (high-speed running or explosive skating stride at full extension). Eccentric hamstring strength is the primary protective factor against hamstring tears, and the walkout builds it without any equipment at all.
transfer: Eccentric hamstring control — major injury prevention for hockey sprinters. Three sets × 5 reps. Slow and controlled — the walk-out is where the hamstring loads, the walk-back is where the core works.
cues: "Walk heels out while in bridge" · "Maintain hip height" · "Walk back in"
mistakes: Hips dropping as feet walk out — the hamstrings must hold the hips up. If they drop, shorten the range. Too fast — slow and controlled eccentric loading is the entire point. Only doing the walk-out without the walk-back — the concentric return also matters. Skipping it because it seems too easy at short range — going to full extension is genuinely hard.
progression: Progress: Single-leg hamstring walkout — one foot elevated, walk out on a single leg. | Regress: Short-range walkout (feet only go out 15-20cm) until full-range hip-hold is achievable.

name: Leg Curl (Machine)
execution: Lie face-down on the leg curl machine. Pad sits just above the heels. Grip the handles for stability. Keep hips flat on the pad throughout. Curl both heels toward the glutes as far as possible. Squeeze the hamstrings hard at full contraction. Pause 1 second. Lower slowly — 3-4 seconds — to full extension. Do not let hips rise off the pad during the curl.
why: The leg curl isolates the hamstrings in knee flexion — the function that decelerates the leg at the end of each skating stride. While deadlifts and RDLs train the hamstrings in hip extension, the leg curl is the only exercise that specifically develops the knee flexion strength that protects the ACL under dynamic loading. NHL injury data consistently shows hamstring-to-quad ratio (ideally above 0.6) as a key ACL injury risk factor.
transfer: Isolates hamstrings — balances quad dominance common in hockey players. Pair leg curl with RDL on the same day for double hamstring stimulus. Insurance against the April pull.
cues: "Curl fully" · "Squeeze at peak contraction" · "Slow lowering phase"
mistakes: Hips lifting off the pad to complete the range — reduces hamstring isolation. Too fast on the way down — the 3-4 second eccentric is where injury prevention happens. Only doing bilateral — add single-leg curls to identify and correct imbalances.',. Going too heavy — proper form requires smooth full-range motion, not grinding.',.
progression: Progress: Nordic curl — the gold standard eccentric hamstring exercise.', | Regress: Hamstring walkout on the floor — same eccentric demand with no machine needed.',

name: Nordic Hamstring Curl
execution: Kneel on a pad, feet anchored under a bar, bench, or held by a partner. Arms crossed on chest or ready to catch you. Body perfectly upright — hips extended, torso in line with thighs. Slowly lower your body FORWARD toward the floor — resist the fall using the hamstrings. Lower as slowly as possible. When you can no longer resist, catch yourself with hands. Push back up with the hands and use the hamstrings to pull back to the upright start.
why: The Nordic curl is the most evidence-based hamstring injury prevention exercise in existence — multiple RCTs show it reduces hamstring strain risk by 51%. It eccentrically loads the hamstring from full knee extension through flexion, exactly the position of maximum strain during explosive skating. NFL, NHL, and soccer teams mandate Nordic curls after injury data became undeniable. Two sessions per week is enough for significant protection.
transfer: The single best exercise to prevent hamstring tears — critical for hockey players. If you can do 12 reps, you're elite. Most pros can do 6-8. Don't rush the standard.
cues: "Kneel" · "Partner holds ankles" · "Lower body as slow as possible" · "Push up with hands"
mistakes: Hips bending — the hips must stay extended. Hinge at the knee only. Dropping too fast — maximum eccentric resistance is the entire stimulus. Only doing the negative — the pull-back concentric also matters. Skipping it because it's hard — the difficulty is proportional to the protection it provides.
progression: Progress: Add a resistance band across the back for more eccentric load on the way down. | Regress: Hamstring walkout on the floor — same eccentric demand with fully bodyweight support.

name: Reverse Nordic Hold
execution: Kneel on a padded surface — folded towel, yoga mat, or carpet works. Knees hip-width, toes pointing back behind you (feet flat or pointed, your choice). Push your hips slightly forward and engage the glutes. Slowly lean backward — body stays in one straight line from knees to head. Stop where it gets hard — your eventual goal is hands able to touch the floor behind you, but start much shallower. HOLD. Tight glutes the whole hold. Return to upright under control.
why: The reverse Nordic is one of the very few exercises that loads the quads in their LENGTHENED position — the same angle the quad reaches at the back end of a hard deceleration or stop, where strains happen. Most quad training (squats, lunges, leg press) loads the muscle in a shortened or mid-range position, leaving the lengthened end of the strength curve untrained. That gap is exactly where injuries occur. A 20-30 second iso hold in the deepest reverse-Nordic position builds tissue tolerance precisely where it's needed for hockey: protecting against quad strains, building tendon stiffness around the kneecap, and adding the kind of bombproof anterior chain that lets a player decelerate from full speed on demand.
transfer: Loads the quads in the LENGTHENED position — the exact angle they fail at during hard decelerations. A rare quality you can't train any other way; protects against quad strains and patellar pain. Don't grind through pinching at the kneecap — that means you've gone too far. Find the position where it's hard but not sharp.
cues: "Kneel on a pad" · "Knees hip-width" · "Toes pointed back. Lean backward as far as you can control — hips push slightly forward" · "Body straight from knees to head. HOLD where it gets hard."
mistakes: Bending at the hips to fake range — defeats the exercise; body stays straight knees-to-head. Going too deep too fast — quad strains happen here; progress 5° per week max. Sharp pinching pain at the kneecap — back off immediately; that means you've gone past tolerance. Skipping the knee pad — bare knees on a hard floor end the set before the quads do.
progression: Progress: Reverse Nordic with arms overhead — adds anterior-chain demand and moment arm. Eventually full bottom range with hands on the floor behind you. | Regress: Shallow reverse Nordic — lean only 15-20° back, hands on thighs for support.

name: Romanian Deadlift (RDL)
execution: Hold a barbell or dumbbells in front of the thighs, arms straight. Stand tall — soft bend in the knees, this is NOT a locked-knee movement. Hinge at the hips: push them BACK while lowering the weight along the legs. Feel the hamstrings stretch as the weight descends to mid-shin. Keep the back flat — same neutral spine as a deadlift setup. Drive the hips forward to return to standing. Squeeze glutes at the top.
why: The Romanian deadlift (RDL) is the premier hamstring and glute strength builder — it trains the hip hinge under load through a large range of motion without the complexity of a conventional deadlift. For hockey players, strong hamstrings from RDLs directly reduce hamstring strain risk during explosive skating, improve stride extension, and build the posterior chain balance needed to offset the quad-dominant skating pattern.
transfer: Builds hamstring and glute strength — drives skating extension. Three seconds down, one second up. The eccentric is where the hamstring grows. Don't bounce.
cues: "Hip hinge" · "Soft knees" · "Bar close to legs" · "Feel hamstrings stretch" · "Drive hips forward"
mistakes: Bending the knees too much — turns it into a deadlift. Keep the slight knee bend consistent. Rounding the lower back — neutral spine throughout. Chest tall. Bar drifting away from the legs — keep it dragging along the shins and thighs. Not going low enough — aim for mid-shin before returning.
progression: Progress: Single-leg RDL — unilateral loading with massive balance and hip stability demand. | Regress: Dumbbell RDL — easier to keep the weight close to the body and control the range.

name: Russian Kettlebell Swing
execution: Stand with feet slightly wider than hip-width. Bell on the floor slightly in front. Hinge at the hips, grip the bell with both hands. Hike the bell back between the legs like a centre snapping a football. Drive the hips FORWARD explosively — stand up fast. The bell floats up. Let the bell float to chest height — it's the hip snap that drives it, not the arms. As the bell falls, hinge back immediately — load for the next rep.
